# Joshua 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1 — The Canaanites' hearts melt

The Amorite and Canaanite kings represent all seven nations of Canaan. The "Amorites" here are those west of the Jordan (distinguished from those east already defeated), and "Canaanites" refers particularly to those dwelling along the Mediterranean coast. The phrase "until **we** had crossed over" hints that the writer was an eyewitness — likely Joshua himself. The kings had heard about the drying up of the Jordan, which they regarded as their natural bulwark during flood season. Their "heart melted" means a complete loss of courage and resistance — they were paralysed with terror, exactly as Rahab had predicted in Joshua 2:9–11. The word "we" in the Hebrew text strongly supports Joshua's authorship. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/5.htm ; Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm)

Donald Campbell (cited on Precept Austin) notes that human military wisdom would have called for an immediate strike while the enemy was demoralised. But God's plan was different: consecration must precede conquest. God is never in a hurry though His children often are. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-5-commentary)

Guzik (Enduring Word) adds that the terror was not merely about military might but about witnessing God's power firsthand. Boice is quoted: "Worldly wisdom would have called for an immediate attack… Instead, God called for a three-day delay while Israel observed the two sacraments." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)

---

## v. 2 — The command to circumcise with flint knives

"At that time" — precisely when the Canaanites were paralysed with fear, making it the providentially appointed moment. The Hebrew is literally "knives of *tsurim*" (rocks/flints). Ellicott notes that authorities are divided: the word *tsûr* may refer to sharpness/keen edge rather than material, though the LXX addition to Joshua 24:30 states stone knives were placed in Joshua's tomb. Gill notes that Maimonides interpreted it as stone knives, and that Jews in the East used stone knives for circumcision even in Gill's day. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm ; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/5.htm)

Guzik explains that flint (obsidian) knives were likely used for ritual significance, connecting to the requirement for unhewn stone altars (Exodus 20:25). Despite Israel's access to metal, God required natural stone — symbolising that human artifice must not touch what belongs to God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)

"Again the second time" — this does not mean re-circumcising those already circumcised (as some Jewish fables suggested), but refers to a second great national circumcision. The first was at the Exodus (either before the first Passover in Egypt or at Sinai before the Passover of Numbers 9:1). From that time until Gilgal, circumcision had been neglected for the 38 years of wilderness wandering. Gill suggests the neglect was due to the uncertainty of travel — they never knew how long they would stay camped, and circumcision required a recovery period. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/5.htm)

---

## v. 3 — Joshua obeys at Gibeath-haaraloth

"Gibeath-haaraloth" means "the hill of the foreskins." Guzik clarifies they did not literally make a hill of foreskins; the site was named afterwards for what happened there. Jewish tradition (Pirke Eliezer, cited by Gill) says the foreskins were heaped and covered with dust, giving the place its name. Joshua did not necessarily perform the circumcisions himself but ordered and oversaw them. Circumcision was never restricted to priests; anyone could perform it. (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/ ; Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/5.htm)

---

## vv. 4–5 — Why circumcision was needed: the Exodus generation had died

All the men of war who came out of Egypt had been circumcised, but they died in the wilderness. Those born during the 40 years had not been circumcised. Guzik notes that it is hard to explain why none were circumcised during those years — circumcision was the covenant sign (Genesis 17:9–14) and was affirmed in the Law (Leviticus 12:3). Yet the text is clear: there were apparently no circumcisions carried out on males during the 38-year wilderness wandering after Sinai. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)

Ellicott offers a distinctive theological explanation: the period between departing Kadesh-barnea and returning to Kadesh (about 37½ years, Numbers 15–19) is a "blank" in the Exodus story. The people had "turned back in their hearts to Egypt" (Acts 7:39) and were bearing the "breach of promise" of Jehovah (Numbers 14:34). They appear to have omitted the covenant sign as though they were no longer God's people. The passage of the Jordan was practical proof of their restoration to divine favour. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm)

The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary (on StudyLight) notes that the omission of circumcision symbolised the spiritual condition of the wilderness generation — disobedience left its mark even on their children's bodies. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-5.html)

---

## v. 6 — The 40 years' wandering as judgment

The 40 years was God's judgment on the Exodus generation for refusing to obey His voice — specifically their unbelief after the spies' report (Numbers 14). The LORD swore they would not see the land. Gill notes this is a round number (actually a few days short of 40 years). "A land flowing with milk and honey" is the covenant promise made to the patriarchs. The use of "us" again suggests an eyewitness author. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/5.htm ; Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes that the text specifies "men of war" — those of the numbering — died under the Lord's judgment. This exempts females and Levites who were not in the numbering, though many of those would have died naturally over 40 years. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/joshua-5.html)

---

## v. 7 — The new generation circumcised

"Their children whom He raised up in their place" — God replaced the unbelieving generation with their sons. These had not been circumcised "along the way" (literally "in the journey"), which as Gill noted, seems to confirm that the itinerant nature of wilderness life was the practical reason for the omission. (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/5.htm)

---

## v. 8 — Faith demonstrated through vulnerability

All the fighting men remained in camp until healed — making the entire army defenceless for several days. Guzik and Schaeffer (cited by Guzik) stress this was an "absolutely unmilitary act." God could have commanded circumcision while they were still east of the Jordan, protected by the river barrier. Instead He waited until they were in enemy territory, making their army defenceless. This required radical trust. The parallel with Genesis 34:24–25 is striking — Simeon and Levi slaughtered the men of Shechem while they were incapacitated after circumcision. Israel faced the same risk but trusted God for protection. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)

Grant's Commentary (Brethren) emphasises the spiritual significance: "If we are going to judge others on God's behalf, we must first learn to judge ourselves." Circumcision represents "no confidence in the flesh" (Philippians 3:3). The cutting off of the flesh is imperative before engaging in any warfare for God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/joshua-5.html)

---

## v. 9 — "The reproach of Egypt" rolled away at Gilgal

"Gilgal" is from the Hebrew root *galal* ("to roll"). God declares He has "rolled away the reproach of Egypt."

**Multiple interpretations exist for "the reproach of Egypt":**

1. **The shame of uncircumcision** (traditional Jewish view, noted by Gill): The Egyptians themselves were uncircumcised at this period; Israel's uncircumcision made them like Egyptians. Now, through obedience, that reproach was removed. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/5.htm)

2. **The reproach of slavery**: Guzik holds this view — the disgrace of their degrading slavery in Egypt was finally lifted as they became a "Promised Land people, not a slave people." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)

3. **The Egyptians' taunt that God led Israel out to destroy them**: Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary, cited on Precept Austin) argues the reproach was the charge that Yahweh had led Israel into the wilderness to destroy them (Exodus 32:12; Numbers 14:13–16; Deuteronomy 9:28). Now that God had brought them into the land, this criticism was negated. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-5-commentary)

4. **The reproach of apostasy**: Ellicott connects it to Israel's "breach of promise" — their turning back to Egypt in their hearts during the wilderness years. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm)

Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) teaches that Egypt represents the flesh-life. The reproach of Egypt is the longing for the "flesh pots of Egypt" — the old life of bondage to fleshly desires. Circumcision typifies cutting away the heart after the flesh (Deuteronomy 30:6). (from Smith's Bible Commentary, retrieved via search excerpt: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/joshua-5.html)

The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics presents circumcision and Passover as "the two sacraments of the old covenant" — circumcision symbolising holiness through crucifixion of the flesh, and Passover representing past and future deliverance. It applies this to the Church: "The Christian should gird himself for the conflict of the spiritual life... by that circumcision of the heart which was the deep truth signified by the old fleshly rite." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/joshua/5.htm)

---

## v. 10 — The Passover celebrated at Gilgal

This is only the third recorded Passover in Israel's history: (1) in Egypt at the Exodus, (2) at Sinai one year later (Numbers 9:1–5), and (3) now at Gilgal. Ellicott observes: "Two belong to the Exodus, or going out; one to the Eisodus, or coming in." The connection to Luke 22:16 is noted — Jesus said He would not eat the Passover again "until it be fulfilled in the kingdom of God." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm)

The timing is precise: they crossed the Jordan on the 10th day of the first month (Joshua 4:19), the day for selecting the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:3). Circumcision took place on the 11th (per Jewish tradition, Seder Olam), allowing three days' healing before the Passover on the 14th at twilight — since the third day after circumcision was the most painful (cf. Genesis 34:25). (Gill: https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/5.htm)

Ellicott stresses the connection between circumcision and Passover: Exodus 12:48 states "no uncircumcised person shall eat thereof." Hence the uncircumcised wilderness generation could not keep the Passover. Now, being circumcised, they could. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm)

Grant's Commentary (Brethren) observes that "circumcision deals with what is negative, the judgment of sin in our own flesh," while "the keeping of the Passover is intended to direct our eyes to the Lord Jesus, the Lamb of God." Only when the flesh is put in its place of death will Christ and His sacrifice receive the honour belonging to Him. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/joshua-5.html)

---

## v. 11 — Eating the produce of the land

The day after Passover (the 15th day of the first month, the start of the Feast of Unleavened Bread), they ate unleavened cakes and parched grain from the land's produce. There is debate about whether this was "old corn" (KJV, following Kimchi and Jewish commentators) or simply "produce of the land" (as the Septuagint renders it). The Jewish commentators argue it must have been old corn because Leviticus 23:10, 14 forbade eating new grain until the wave-sheaf offering (16th of Nisan). Gill discusses this tension but notes the Septuagint simply says "corn of the land." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/5.htm)

The Pulpit Homiletics draws a striking parallel: "They not only had in this feast a pledge of the promised deliverance, but an earnest of the good things to come... The same thing is true of the Christian sacrament. While it is an essentially spiritual feast, it still gives in part that which it sets forth and symbolises. Faith receives the Holy Spirit in baptism, and feeds upon the invisible Christ in the Lord's Supper." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/joshua/5.htm)

---

## v. 12 — The manna ceases

The manna ceased on the day after they ate the land's produce — the 16th day of the first month. Ellicott notes a "remarkable coincidence": the manna first appeared on the 16th day of the second month of the first year of the Exodus (Exodus 16:1, 13–14). It fell for 39 years and 11 months, always resting on the Sabbath. It finally ceased (*vay-yishboth* — "kept Sabbath") on the very day later marked by Christ's resurrection, which became the Lord's Day. Ellicott sees this as typology: "It is the risen Christ who takes the place of the manna" (cf. John 6:39–40, 44, 54). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm)

Guzik emphasises that God did not want Israel to become lazy; He transitioned them from miraculous provision to a "new partnership of trust" where they would cooperate through their own labour. Morgan is quoted: "God never employs supernatural methods of supplying needs which can be met by natural means." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)

Gill notes that the ceasing of the manna proves it was not a natural phenomenon but an extraordinary provision. He then draws an eschatological analogy: manna (a type of Christ in Gospel ordinances) will cease when the saints enter the heavenly Canaan — replaced by the "fruit of the land," the eternal joys prepared from the foundation of the world. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/5.htm)

---

## v. 13 — Joshua meets the Commander with drawn sword

This verse introduces the second major division of the book (the Conquest). Joshua is near Jericho — perhaps reconnoitring, meditating, or praying. He sees "a Man" standing opposite him with a drawn sword. The drawn sword in Scripture appears elsewhere with the angel who stopped Balaam (Numbers 22:23) and the angel ready to execute judgment for David's census (1 Chronicles 21:16) — it signals imminent divine judgment. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm ; Guzik citing Hess: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)

Joshua's question — "Are You for us or for our adversaries?" — was logical for a military leader. But the answer he receives ("Neither" / "No") reframes everything.

---

## v. 14 — "Neither… but as Commander of the LORD's army"

**The "No" / "Neither" answer is theologically significant.** Ellicott explains it masterfully: Jehovah will take part in this conflict not as an ally or an adversary, but as Commander-in-Chief. "It is not Israel's quarrel, in which they are to ask the Divine assistance. It is the Lord's own quarrel, and Israel and Joshua are but a division in His host." The wars of Israel in Canaan are always presented as "the wars of the LORD." This is crucial for understanding the conquest ethically: the war is a divine enterprise, not merely a human act of aggression. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm)

Guzik puts it more simply: the proper question wasn't whether God was on Joshua's side, but whether Joshua was on God's side. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)

Joshua worships the Man — falling facedown — and the Man receives it. This is a key Christological point: mere angels refuse worship (Revelation 22:8–9), but this figure accepts it. Guzik and the broad conservative tradition identify this as a Christophany — a pre-incarnate appearance of God the Son. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)

Chuck Smith concurs: "Here Joshua met Jesus, Jesus the Captain of the Lord's host… If it were an angel then He would've refused his worship." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/joshua-5.html)

Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) emphasises the drawn sword being in *His* hand, not an angel's or minister's: "Oh, what power there is in the gospel when Jesus holds the hilt." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary concurs: "He was face to face with the Lord in the guise of an armed warrior." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/joshua-5.html)

---

## v. 15 — "Take off your sandals… holy ground"

The identical command given to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:5) confirms the identity of the Speaker as the same divine Person. Ellicott contrasts the two theophanies: the burning bush (not consumed) pictured suffering Israel in affliction with God suffering alongside them. The drawn sword is the sign of victory — "Jehovah no longer suffers with and in His people, but He stands forth to lead them with the drawn sword." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm)

Precept Austin summarises: "Here was the Warrior and Leader, coming not to help but to take charge." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-5-commentary)

---

## Points of Difference Between Protestant Traditions

### 1. The identity of the "Commander of the LORD's army" (vv. 13–15)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik, Chuck Smith):** Unambiguously identifies the figure as the pre-incarnate Jesus Christ. Emphasis on worship being accepted as proof of deity, and on the personal relationship — Joshua meets his Captain. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)
- **Reformed/Baptist (Gill):** Identifies the figure as "a divine Person… the Son of God," noting that ancient Jewish interpreters identified him as "Michael the uncreated angel, the head of all principality and power" — i.e., the eternal Word. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/5.htm)
- **Anglican/Older (Ellicott):** Identifies the figure as the "Angel of Jehovah" — a theophany — and emphasises the theological significance of the encounter over the identity question. The focus is on how this vision inaugurates the conquest as a divine enterprise. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm)
- **Plymouth Brethren (Grant):** Focuses on the practical spiritual lesson: God intended to impress on Joshua that "he was only a" subordinate. The emphasis is on Christ's supremacy, not speculative identification. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/joshua-5.html)

### 2. Circumcision and its relationship to baptism (vv. 2–9)

- **Baptist (Guzik/Enduring Word):** Explicitly argues against paedobaptism: "It is wrong and harmful to make the analogy, 'babies were circumcised, so babies should be baptized.'" The new covenant is entered by spiritual birth, not physical birth. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)
- **Reformed (implied through Pulpit Homiletics and Constable):** Draws a parallel between circumcision and baptism as covenant signs, with the Pulpit Commentary calling circumcision and Passover "the two sacraments of the old covenant" — language that leans toward a sacramental understanding. Constable notes circumcision "brought the individual male under the blessings of the Abrahamic Covenant" — a corporate, covenant-family understanding. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/joshua/5.htm ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-5-commentary)

### 3. The meaning of "the reproach of Egypt" (v. 9)

- **Traditional Jewish/Kimchi (cited by Gill):** The reproach of uncircumcision — being like the uncircumcised Egyptians. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/5.htm)
- **Dispensational/Evangelical (Constable, Guzik):** The Egyptians' taunt that God led Israel out to destroy them, now silenced by their entry into the land. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-5-commentary)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Chuck Smith):** The flesh-life — Egypt symbolises living after the flesh. The reproach is longing for "the flesh pots of Egypt." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/joshua-5.html)
- **Anglican (Ellicott):** The reproach of apostasy during the wilderness years — "the breach of promise" of Jehovah. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm)

### 4. Flint knives: literal stone or idiom? (v. 2)

- **Baptist (Gill):** Favours literal stone knives, citing Maimonides, the LXX, and contemporary Jewish practice. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/5.htm)
- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Suggests "knives of keen edge" may be the better translation, with *tsûr* referring to sharpness rather than material — though concedes they may have been stone in practice. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/5.htm)
- **Pentecostal (Guzik):** Accepts stone (obsidian) knives as historically and ritually significant, paralleling the unhewn stone altar requirement. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship

The search results and fetches from the approved sites did not return specific modernist/critical scholarship content from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org notes for Joshua 5. However, Richard Hess (cited by Guzik on Enduring Word) represents an evangelical scholarly voice, noting that obsidian knives "enjoyed popularity for ritual and non-ritual purposes long after the development of metal knives" and that "Amorites and Canaanites are terms used to describe the same peoples" with their locations identifying "all the areas of the land." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-5/)

## Summary of the Chapter's Structure

Jensen (cited on Precept Austin) outlines the chapter as "Spiritual Preparation" with four tokens:
1. **Token of Circumcision** (vv. 2–9): Restoration to covenant favour
2. **Token of Blood** (v. 10): Anticipation of deliverance (Passover)
3. **Token of Fruit** (vv. 11–12): Appropriation of the blessings
4. **Token of a Sword** (vv. 13–15): Revelation of a holy war

(https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-5-commentary)

Don Anderson (also on Precept Austin) summarises the chapter as four "new" things: a new POSITION (circumcision), a new BEGINNING (Passover), a new FOOD (produce of the land), and a new CAPTAIN (the Commander of the Lord's army). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-5-commentary)
